scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Here’s my perspective, rooted in biblical principles: ### **Is it wrong to refuse to cook for your mom?** **Not necessarily—but it depends on the heart behind it and how it’s handled.** Here’s why: 1. **Fairness & Shared Responsibility (Colossians 3:19, Titus 2:4-5)** - The Bible calls for **mutual respect and shared burdens** in the home. If your mom is not contributing fairly (e.g., watching TV all day, not cooking, expecting you to do all the work), it’s reasonable to question why *she* isn’t helping. - Your dad does **most of the cooking and chores**, which is commendable, but if your mom is also at home, she should share the load. If she refuses to learn or help, that’s a problem. 2. **Your Burden of Schoolwork (Galatians 6:5, Matthew 11:28-30)** - Jesus didn’t call us to **burn out** under impossible demands. If your mom is expecting you to cook **every night** while you have heavy schoolwork, that’s unreasonable. - You’re not wrong for prioritizing your education—**God values wisdom and diligence** (Proverbs 16:3, 18:15). 3. **Her Expectations vs. Reality (Ephesians 4:29, Proverbs 15:1)** - Your mom’s reaction was **unfair and harsh**. She should have considered: - That you’re in school (not just "home all day"). - That she’s the one who **chooses not to cook** (despite your dad’s efforts to teach her). - That **her own laziness** (watching TV all day) contributes to the problem. - **Constructive criticism is kind (Galatians 6:1)**, but **shaming and yelling** are not love in action. 4. **Your Dad’s Role (Ephesians 5:22-33, 1 Timothy 5:8)** - Your dad is a **great example** of a husband who provides for his family (1 Timothy 5:8). However, **a healthy home requires teamwork**. - If your mom is **not pulling her weight**, your dad should **gently but firmly** address this with her—not just rely on you and your sister. --- ### **What Would Be a Better Approach?** Instead of **passive resistance** (not cooking and expecting him to fix it), try this: ✅ **1. Have a Calm, Respectful Conversation with Your Mom** - *"Mom, I understand you’re tired after work, but I’m also doing a lot of schoolwork now. Can we figure out a fair way to share dinner responsibilities? Maybe you could cook a few nights a week, or we could take turns?"* - If she refuses, **politely but firmly** say: *"I can’t keep cooking every night when I have schoolwork. If you’re not going to help, then I can’t either."* ✅ **2. Involve Your Dad (If She Won’t Listen)** - Your dad is a **strong leader** in the home. He should **set expectations** with your mom: - *"Honey, we need to share dinner duties. You’re home early—can you cook a few nights?"* - If she still refuses, he should **stop enabling her laziness** and **take over more** (since he’s already doing most of the cooking). ✅ **3. Set Boundaries (But with Love)** - If she **continues to demand dinner every night** without contributing, you can say: *"I can’t keep cooking for you when I have schoolwork. If you want dinner, you’ll have to make it yourself or ask Dad to help."* - **But also offer help when you can** (e.g., *"I can cook tonight if you help with cleanup"*). ✅ **4. Teach Her (If She’s Willing to Learn)** - If your mom **genuinely wants to cook better**, offer to help her learn (since she refuses to put in effort). - If she **refuses to learn**, then she has to accept the consequences (eating what’s available). --- ### **Final Verdict: Was Your Reaction "AITA"?** **Not entirely wrong—but it could have been handled better.** - **You were right to push back**—she was being unfair. - **You were right to expect fairness**—she’s not pulling her weight. - **But yelling and shaming you was wrong**—she should have communicated better. **A better response would be:** ✔ **Firm but kind** (not passive-aggressive). ✔ **Involving your dad** (since he’s the head of the household). ✔ **Setting clear boundaries** (but not burning bridges). --- ### **Biblical Takeaway:** - **Love requires truth (Ephesians 4:15)**—you can’t just ignore unfairness. - **Wisdom means knowing when to speak and when to walk away (Proverbs 15:1, 29:11).** - **Fairness matters (Deuteronomy 25:13-15)**—no one should be expected to do all the work. - **Grace means giving her a chance to change (Galatians 6:1)**—but if she won’t, you can’t keep enabling her. **Would I give you a 0 or 1?** **1 (with conditions).** - **You were right to stand up for yourself**—but **how you handled it could have been more constructive**. - **The real issue is your mom’s laziness and lack of effort**—not just your refusal to cook. - **Your dad needs to step up as the leader** and **your mom needs to change her attitude**. Would you like help drafting a script for talking to her? I’m happy to help!
